Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) closed at $242.45 on October 19. The stock returned 30.2% over the last 6 months, compared with an 11.6% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 8.7% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.

Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) closed at $129.59 the same day and has gone the other way, shedding more than a quarter of its value over those six months. Two of the largest businesses in enterprise software, pulled apart by half a year of trading. Salesforce sells the system companies run their customer relationships through. Oracle sells databases and rents out the computing capacity that artificial intelligence models are trained on.

READ ALSO: 10 Best Fundamental Stocks to Invest in According to Billionaires

Salesforce (CRM) vs Oracle (ORCL): Which Is a Better Stock to Buy?
What Salesforce Has:

The customer record lives in Salesforce, and so do the workflows the sales and service teams run on top of it. Replacing that means moving years of history and retraining the people who use it daily, which is why a slowing Salesforce is not a shrinking one. It converts about a fifth of revenue into operating profit and produced $14.4 billion of free cash flow in its last financial year.

What it lacks is growth. Revenue rose 10.80% in the most recent quarter, and the company is now buying what it cannot generate, agreeing on October 20 to pay $5.66 billion for the marketing software business Braze. The bigger risk sits in how it charges. Salesforce sells seats, so if software agents take on work that staff used to do, customers need fewer of them.

Both names appear in our 10 Most Promising Cloud Stocks According to Hedge Funds. To see the full ranking, click HERE.

What Oracle Has:

Oracle grew revenue 29.60% in the quarter just reported on a 35.63% operating margin, and underneath that sits the oldest annuity in software. Companies keep their most important records in Oracle databases, and the support that goes with them renews whether or not anything new is bought. That revenue pays for the build. What the market is being asked to price is the newer half, where Oracle rents capacity to companies training artificial intelligence models on contracts signed years in advance.

The build is the risk. Debt reaches 251.72% of equity, more than twice what Salesforce carries, and Oracle finished the past year with levered free cash flow of negative $45.85 billion despite generating a great deal from operations. Renting capacity also earns a thinner margin than licensing software, so faster revenue is not automatically the better business.

Oracle's cloud infrastructure revenue surged 121%, but free cash flow burned $5.4 billion last quarter with no recovery timeline from management.

Oracle has fallen 32% year to date while the S&P 500 gained 13%, yet the average analyst price target implies 81% upside.

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) trades at $131.14. Its low multiple used to look like a bargain, but now it looks like a fair price for a company that has to borrow and issue stock to build its AI cloud.

Maksim Safaniuk / Shutterstock.com

Oracle sells databases, enterprise applications and, more and more, AI training and inference capacity. Cloud now makes up 60% of total revenue, up from 48% a year ago. The stock has fallen 52.08% over the past year and sits far below its 52-week high of $283.40.

A Cheap Multiple Attached to Triple-Digit Infrastructure Growth

Bulls point to the price. At about 16x the $8.10 non-GAAP EPS guide for this fiscal year, and roughly 12x the $10.9916 consensus for next year, Oracle costs less than many slower-growing software names. Its PEG ratio is 0.807.

The growth is real. Cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% to $7.39 billion, and remaining performance obligations reached $664 billion. GPU use was 97.9%, and renewed capacity was repriced at a 20% premium to prior contracts. Analysts made 35 upward and 1 downward full-year EPS revisions over the past 30 days.

Negative Free Cash Flow Is Eating the Growth Story

Free cash flow was negative $5.4 billion last quarter, following negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026. Management still expects $90 billion to $95 billion in capex this year. Interest expense rose 55% to $1.4 billion. After completing a $20 billion equity sale, Oracle plans to raise about $40 billion more through debt and equity.

title: Why Did Braze Stock Jump?
detail:
Why Did Braze Stock Jump?
Trefis Team

Braze (BRZE) stock rose 51.7% on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, while the S&P 500 gained 0.3%. The gain occurred the same day news reports said Salesforce had agreed to buy the customer-engagement software company for cash. Braze shareholders now know what they would be paid, allowing that price to be measured against the business Salesforce is buying. So how much is Salesforce paying, set against what Braze sells for today?

How Much Is Salesforce Paying For Braze?

News reports on October 20 said Salesforce will pay $47.50 in cash for each Braze share, a 58% premium to the previous close. The same reports valued the deal at $5.66 billion.

For that price, Salesforce would get a company with $834 million of revenue over the twelve months to July 31, 2026, up 27.4% from a year earlier. Over the same four quarters, Salesforce's own revenue grew 11.2%, meaning the buyer is paying for a business growing more than twice as fast as its own. Management said on the September 8, 2026 call that Braze also counted 361 large customers, with each spending at least $500,000 a year.

How Has The Deal Changed What Braze Shares Cost?

Braze shares now cost far more against the company's sales than they did three weeks earlier, and not solely because of the offer. Before the deal news, the stock had already risen about 18% between September 21 and the October 19 close. At the October 20 close, Braze carried a market value of $5.07 billion, or 6.1 times its revenue over the last twelve months. That compares with 3.3 times at the end of September, while the S&P 500 as a whole trades at 3.1 times sales.

The shares closed at $45.57, about 4% below the offer price. That gap suggests the market expects the deal to close but is pricing in some risk or delay.

Braze Still Grows Fast And Still Reports A Loss

Salesforce is buying the business Braze described when it last reported on that September 8 call. Over the twelve months to July 31, 2026, Braze still reported an operating loss equal to 13.4% of revenue, though that loss was narrower than the 20.3% of a year earlier. The company also produced $80.2 million of free cash flow over those twelve months.

During that call, management guided fiscal Q3 2027 revenue to between $229 million and $230 million, up from the $227 million Braze reported for fiscal Q2 2027. They also raised the full-year guide, projecting revenue of $910 million to $913 million for fiscal 2027. The offer changes none of those figures.

Larry Ellison, co-founder of Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), put up shares of Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) and SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) as collateral this year. He used them to borrow more from banks and help pay for his son David Ellison's takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. The Wall Street Journal reported the pledges on October 20, 2026, citing filings.

24/7 Wall St.

The Tesla and SpaceX pledges are reported, and the companies have not confirmed them. No share counts, loan amounts, or lender names have been made public.

Oracle closed at $131.14 on October 20, up 1.16% for the session. Tesla rose 1.54% to $373.71 after Elon Musk commented on a possible SpaceX merger. SpaceX closed at $147.79 and then reached $159.70 after hours on its third-quarter results. Those moves follow earnings and merger news. Nothing in them points to the collateral report.

Why a Falling Stock Can Force a Borrower to Sell

In a stock-backed loan, a bank lends cash against shares. If the shares fall far enough, the borrower has to post more collateral or sell stock.

Billionaires borrow because selling triggers capital gains tax and cuts their voting control. The collateral's value now moves with three volatile stocks, adding risk. SpaceX just reported, and Tesla reports third-quarter results after the close on October 21.

Oracle's Proxy Shows a Growing Pledge

As of the September 21 record date, Ellison beneficially owned 1,158,375,174 Oracle shares, or 38.2% of the class. He has pledged 413,000,000 of them, up from 346 million a year earlier.

title: Is Veeva Systems Stock Really Expensive?

Is Veeva Systems Stock Really Expensive?

Image from Pixabay

Veeva Systems (VEEV) stock trades at 51 times its earnings over the last twelve months, compared with 23 for the S&P 500. The shares returned 72.7% from July 22 to October 20, 2026. Buyers entering the market after a rally like that are paying today for profit the business has not yet earned. How fast would Veeva have to grow for that price to hold?

Veeva Would Need Faster Growth Than It Delivers

At this price, Veeva would have to grow revenue 18.8% a year for five years. By comparison, revenue grew 16.5% in the twelve months to July 31, 2026. So the shares look somewhat expensive: dear against today's growth, though not by a wide margin.

Three Trefis assumptions dictate that 18.8% rate, none of them observed in the market or stated by the company. Trefis calculates a mature P/E of 22.8 by combining a fixed 18.0 level for healthcare stocks with Veeva's own average P/E. The formula weights the healthcare level at 60% and Veeva's average at 40%. Veeva averaged 49.4 over the last twelve quarter ends. Trefis caps any company average above 30 at 30, so the mature multiple uses 30 in place of Veeva's 49.4.

Veeva closed October 20, 2026, with a market value of $51.7 billion. At the mature P/E, that valuation requires net income of $2.27 billion. Assuming a steady net margin of 27.7%, Veeva would need $8.19 billion in revenue to earn that profit. The 27.7% margin sits halfway between Veeva's 26.1% average and its 29.3% high over the last twelve quarter ends. Trefis allows five years because today's P/E is 2.24 times the mature one, and its rule assigns five years to any ratio from two up to three. Bridging the gap from today's $3.46 billion in revenue to that $8.19 billion target demands 18.8% annual growth.

Does Veeva's Guidance Point To Growth That Fast?

No, not even for fiscal 2027. Management guided revenue of $3.68 billion to $3.69 billion for fiscal 2027, an increase from its June guide of $3.64 billion. The midpoint of that range marks 15.3% growth over fiscal 2026. After fiscal 2027, Veeva would have to grow 19.4% a year until fiscal Q2 2032, faster than the pace management has guided for fiscal 2027. Management said on the August 26 call that it would not guide beyond fiscal 2027.

Subscriptions account for most of the business. The Subscription segment brought in $2.68 billion in fiscal 2026, up 17.5% from a year earlier. On the same call, management said three large companies had selected Vault CRM. Management also raised its fiscal 2027 guide for adjusted operating income to $1.64 billion from $1.61 billion, so the profit outlook rose along with revenue.

Oracle trades at 18x earnings with a $249 analyst price target, but a junk credit downgrade would crush the bull case.

On October 20, 2026, TD Cowen analyst Michael Elias wrote that Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) may be helping Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) secure lender funding for its AI data centers. Neither company has confirmed this, and the size of any support remains unquantified.

Shutterstock

Oracle closed at $131.14, up 1.20%. Nvidia fell 0.29% to $216.47. Oracle's small gain follows a 52.06% drop over the year. The stock is much cheaper, but the company may now be relying on its largest chip supplier to keep building.

Two Ways Nvidia Could Back Oracle's Leases

Elias based his view on channel checks, which means conversations with people in the industry. He found that Nvidia may be giving Oracle "credit support" in one of two ways.

The first is a credit guarantee. Nvidia would stand behind Oracle's lease payments, so data center owners still get paid if Oracle runs into trouble; the second is a sublease in which Nvidia would lease the buildings itself and then rent them to Oracle. In both cases, lenders would be counting on Nvidia's stronger credit, which makes them more willing to fund construction.

Elias linked the agreement to Oracle's reported five-year deal with Tencent. Under that deal, Tencent would lease about 100,000 advanced AI chips in Oracle data centers in Southeast Asia. The lease is estimated at about $7 billion, with roughly 30% paid upfront. That deal is still unconfirmed, and the countries involved have not been disclosed.
